introduction-building-people-not-just-pr.core: Senior engineers multiply impact by growing others: mentoring, sponsoring, making career paths clear, spreading knowledge and planning succession. A team that depends on one expert is fragile.

first_principles.problem: A senior engineer ships great work alone, while the team's skills stagnate and everything depends on them.

analogy.title: A master chef running a kitchen
analogy.story: Their job isn't just cooking the best dish but training the line so every plate is excellent.
analogy.breaks: Growing others takes time from your own delivery, which is an investment, not a loss.

example.title: A senior's impact over a year
flow: Multiplier: ships 5, grows 3 engineers who ship 30
example.outcome: impact measured by the team's growth.

check.q: Why is growing others part of a senior engineer's job?
check.a: It multiplies impact beyond individual output and reduces dependency on any one person.

mentorship-vs-sponsorship-knowing-the-di.core: Mentorship is advice and guidance: talking with someone about how to grow. Sponsorship is advocacy: using your influence to get them opportunities, visibility and promotions. Sponsorship costs political capital and drives career outcomes.

first_principles.problem: Underrepresented engineers get plenty of mentoring but little sponsorship, so they're advised but not advanced.
truths: Visibility and stretch opportunities drive promotions.
derivation: **Sponsor**: nominate for projects, speak up in calibration, amplify wins.

analogy.title: A coach vs. an agent
analogy.story: A coach improves your game; an agent gets you onto the big stage.
analogy.breaks: Sponsoring someone unready can hurt them, so pair sponsorship with mentoring.

example.title: Sponsorship in action
flow: Mentoring on system design for 6 months
Sponsor nominates them to lead cross-team RFC
example.outcome: careers actively advanced, not just advised.

check.q: What's the key difference between mentorship and sponsorship?
check.a: Mentorship gives advice; sponsorship uses the sponsor's influence to create opportunities and advocate for the person.

career-ladders-the-map-to-growth.core: A career ladder defines levels with concrete expectations (scope, impact, technical skill, collaboration, leadership), often with parallel individual-contributor and management tracks, so growth and promotion are transparent and fair.

first_principles.problem: Promotions feel arbitrary, people don't know what 'senior' means, and bias fills the vacuum.
truths: ICs shouldn't have to manage to advance.
derivation: Define **levels** by scope (task → project → team → org).
Offer **IC and manager tracks** in parallel.

analogy.title: A map with landmarks
analogy.story: Without landmarks, nobody knows how far they've travelled or which way to go next.
analogy.breaks: Ladders can become checkbox exercises, so assess impact, not activities.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Everyone knows what the next level looks like.

check.q: Why have a parallel IC track?
check.a: So engineers can advance in seniority and impact without having to become managers.

knowledge-transfer-avoiding-the-bus-fact.core: The bus factor is the number of people who'd have to disappear before a system becomes unmaintainable. Raise it with documentation, pairing, rotations, shared on-call, recorded walkthroughs and deliberate cross-training.

first_principles.problem: Only one engineer understands the payment service, and their vacation becomes an operational risk.
truths: Single points of failure exist in people too.

analogy.title: A band with one person who knows the songs
analogy.story: If the lead guitarist gets sick, the show is cancelled unless others learned the parts.
analogy.breaks: Full redundancy for everything is costly, so prioritise critical systems.

example.title: Raising a bus factor from 1 to 3

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The expert can take a holiday safely.

check.q: What does a bus factor of 1 mean?
check.a: Only one person understands a system, so losing them would leave it unmaintainable.

succession-planning-thinking-two-moves-a.core: Succession planning means proactively preparing people to step into critical roles (tech lead, on-call lead, your own role) before they're needed, so departures and promotions don't create gaps.

first_principles.problem: A tech lead leaves suddenly, nobody is ready, and the team stalls for months.
truths: Growing successors also frees you to grow.

analogy.title: A chess player thinking two moves ahead
analogy.story: You position pieces now for the situation that will arise later.
analogy.breaks: Succession planning must stay transparent and fair, not favouritism.

example.title: Preparing a successor tech lead
flow: Smooth transition when lead moves on

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No gap, and the team keeps momentum.

check.q: Why does succession planning benefit the current role holder?
check.a: Developing a successor frees them to take on bigger roles without leaving a gap behind.
